candidates.taskText: I run a 14-person structural engineering firm that's been subcontracting to two large construction companies for eight years. One of them has just offered to buy us outright for $2.1M plus retention bonuses for me and my two senior engineers over three years. Separately, the other construction company wants to sign us to an exclusive five-year supply contract at rates 20% above what we currently charge, but it would mean turning down all other client work, including some public-sector jobs we've been chasing for years. Both offers expire at the end of this month because both companies are finalising their own annual budgets. If I sell, I lose control but get certainty and a payout. If I sign the exclusive contract, I keep the business but I'm betting our entire future on one client's continued goodwill. My two senior engineers have said they'd probably leave within a year if we sell, which the acquirer knows and has priced in. I need to decide which path to commit to before the month is out.

My wife and I own a 40-room seaside hotel that's been in the family for three generations. A regional hotel group has offered to lease the building from us for 15 years at a fixed rent that would give us more stable income than we've had in a decade, but we'd give up day-to-day control and our staff of 22 would be transferred to their management. Alternatively, a tourism-board grant has come through that would cover 60% of a renovation to reposition the hotel as a boutique property, but we'd need to take on debt for the rest and run it ourselves for at least another ten years to pay it off. Both options need a decision within five weeks because the lease offer has a deadline and the grant funding must be claimed this fiscal year or it's reallocated elsewhere. We're both in our late fifties and neither of us wants to be doing this hands-on past 65. Which direction should we commit to?

We've already decided to move our regional distribution centre from its current 40,000 sq ft leased site to a new 65,000 sq ft owned facility 12 miles away — the lease and purchase are signed. The new site has three loading docks versus the current five, but double the racking capacity, and it's arranged over two floors instead of one, connected by two freight lifts. We handle around 1,800 outbound pallets a day at peak, with inbound receiving concentrated in the morning and outbound dispatch concentrated in the afternoon. We need to be fully moved and operating out of the new site within eight weeks, ideally without more than a two-day disruption to any single customer's deliveries. We have 34 warehouse staff, three shift supervisors, and a fixed budget for temporary agency labour of $18,000 for the whole transition. Given the dock and lift constraints, how should we sequence the actual move and phase the ramp-up of operations at the new site?

Our regional exam board has committed to moving from paper-based marking to a fully digital marking platform for next year's exam cycle — the software contract is signed and the board has approved the switch. We have 340 markers across the region, most of whom have never used the platform, marking scripts for 22 different subjects with staggered exam dates between May and June. The platform vendor can run live training sessions for at most 40 markers at a time, and each session takes half a day. Scripts for the earliest subjects start arriving for marking three weeks after exams begin, and markers need to have completed training and a standardisation exercise before they can start. We also need at least two senior examiners per subject to have signed off on the standardisation samples before general marking opens for that subject. Given these constraints and our marker numbers, how should we schedule training, standardisation, and the marking start dates across subjects?

I inherited my grandfather's leather goods workshop, which has spent 50 years making work boots and belts for farmers and tradespeople under the name Halden & Sons. Younger customers browsing our new online store keep telling us the name and the old logo — a plough motif from the 1970s — feel irrelevant to them, and we're losing sales to newer brands that look more contemporary, even though our stitching and materials are objectively better. But our existing trade customers, who still make up 70% of our revenue, specifically tell us they buy from us because we look exactly like what we've always looked like — they distrust anything that seems 'redesigned.' We can't afford to run two separate identities, and we're not walking away from either customer base. I need a view on how the brand should present itself now, given both audiences have to see the same name and the same shopfront.

I opened a neighbourhood wine bar eighteen months ago and named it after the street it's on, which felt safe but has turned out to be forgettable — customers keep calling it 'that wine place' rather than by its actual name, and I get almost no word-of-mouth referrals because people can't remember what to tell their friends. The interior has a warm, slightly worn, mismatched-furniture feel that regulars love, but our social media presence and signage still look generic, like a template that could belong to any bar. I'm not changing the food or drinks concept, and I'm not moving locations. I have a modest amount saved to redo signage, the website, and social presence, but I want to get the direction right before spending it, since I can't afford to do it twice. What should the bar's name, voice and visual identity actually be built around?

Our mid-sized call centre switched three months ago from a fixed-schedule shift system to a self-scheduling app where staff pick their own shifts within coverage rules. Since then, average handle time has dropped from 6.2 to 5.4 minutes and customer satisfaction scores have risen from 78% to 84%. But in the same quarter, we also raised the starting hourly wage by $1.50 to stay competitive with a new distribution centre that opened nearby, and we lost our two lowest-performing team leads to resignation, replacing them with two experienced hires from a competitor. Sick-day absence has stayed flat throughout. I've been asked by leadership to explain what's driving the improvement in handle time and satisfaction, since they want to know before deciding whether to roll the self-scheduling system out to our other two centres, which don't have the wage increase or the same staffing changes. What does this data actually tell us about the cause of the improvement?

A community health clinic ran a six-month pilot where patients with type 2 diabetes were given a text-message medication reminder service. Among the 120 patients enrolled, average blood sugar control (HbA1c) improved in 68% of them, compared to a historical baseline where only 45% of similar patients improved over a comparable period. However, enrollment in the pilot was voluntary and required patients to have a mobile phone and be willing to opt in, which excluded about a third of the clinic's diabetic patients who don't have reliable phone access or declined to participate. The pilot also coincided with a separate initiative where the clinic extended nurse follow-up call availability to weekends, which applied to all diabetic patients, not just those in the texting pilot. The clinic's board wants to fund a full rollout of the texting service to all 640 diabetic patients next year based on this pilot. What does the pilot data actually show about the reminder service's effect, and is it sufficient to justify that decision?

My physiotherapy clinic wants to launch a monthly membership for people managing chronic back and joint pain, instead of relying only on one-off appointment bookings. We have four therapists, each with capacity for roughly 25 client hours a week, and we already run a small gym area with equipment that's underused outside peak hours. Competing clinics nearby offer either pure pay-per-session or unlimited-visit memberships, and we don't want to match either exactly. We want something that keeps clients coming back consistently, since adherence is the biggest driver of actual outcomes for this kind of pain, but we can't offer unlimited 1:1 sessions without needing to hire more staff immediately, which we're not ready to commit to. We do have spare gym floor capacity and could offer supervised group sessions relatively cheaply. What should the membership actually include, and how should it be tiered or structured?

We run a small software company that sells an invoicing tool to freelancers, priced as a single flat monthly fee for full access to everything. Support tickets show that most freelancers only use about a third of the features — invoicing, basic expense tracking, and payment reminders — while a smaller group of power users, mostly small agencies with a few employees, want deeper features like multi-user access, approval workflows, and reporting, which we currently include for everyone even though only about 15% of users touch them. Building and maintaining those advanced features costs us real engineering time that isn't reflected in what most customers pay for. We're not looking to change our target market or pricing philosophy dramatically, and we're not asking whether to build new features — we already have a roadmap for that. What we need to figure out is what should actually be included in the base offering versus held back for a higher tier, and how the service should be structured around those two groups of users.

Our small architecture firm received an unexpected $180,000 year-end profit share, and I need to decide how to allocate it across three requests that have all landed on my desk this week. Our senior project lead wants $70,000 to fund her long-planned move into sustainable-materials consulting as a new internal specialty, which she believes will bring in new clients within a year. Our operations manager wants $60,000 to replace our aging project-management and billing software, which currently causes repeated invoicing errors and has already cost us one client dispute this year. And two of our associates have asked for the money to go toward long-overdue salary increases and bonuses, arguing that we've been below-market for two years and are at real risk of losing them to competitors who've already made offers. We don't have more money coming until next year's revenue comes in, and whatever we don't allocate now will just sit as retained earnings until then. How should the $180,000 be divided among these three claims?

I manage the annual training budget for a 90-person engineering department, and this year we have $95,000 to allocate, down from $140,000 last year because of company-wide cuts. Three things are competing for it. First, a mandatory safety recertification for 30 field engineers costs $28,000 and has to happen regardless, since it's a regulatory requirement. Second, our cloud infrastructure team of 12 wants $45,000 for a specialised certification program they say is essential given we're migrating our entire platform next year and none of them are currently certified on the new systems. Third, a broader request from across the department for $50,000 worth of general conference attendance and professional development stipends, which staff have consistently cited in exit interviews as something they value and feel we've cut too aggressively in recent years. The recertification is non-negotiable. Beyond that, I need to decide how to split the remaining $67,000 between the infrastructure certification and the broader professional development requests.
